finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 3 scored permit indicators in Bedford Dwellings moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

New residential construction permits: 16 in 2023–2025 vs. 0 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 0 would be expected. Declared value of residential building permits: $4.4M in 2023–2025 vs. $672K in 2020–2022 (+552%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $747K would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: new construction (2025, higher), then permit value (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 18 vacant lots here (39.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Bedford Dwellings saw far more new-home building activity than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Bedford Dwellings had 16 permits to build new homes in 2023–2025, compared with 0 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, permits to build new homes citywide went down 11%.

In Bedford Dwellings, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $672K (2020–2022) to $4.4M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2025, when permits to build new homes rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Low — there are few permits here or the signals are mixed, so one project can swing the numbers. Many of these permits were issued on the same day, which usually means one large multi-lot project.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
plain.similar_text: Other neighborhoods with a similar pattern: Esplen, Central Oakland, Ridgemont.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 3 of 4 scored permit indicators in Allentown moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

New residential construction permits: 31 in 2023–2025 vs. 2 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 2 would be expected. Declared value of residential building permits: $7.2M in 2023–2025 vs. $1.2M in 2020–2022 (+506%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $1.3M would be expected. Residential renovation / alteration permits: 79 in 2023–2025 vs. 44 in 2020–2022 (+80%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 49 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2022, lower), then new construction (2024, higher), then demolitions (2024, higher), then renovations (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 121 vacant lots here (158.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.headline: Allentown saw far more new-home building activity than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Allentown had 31 permits to build new homes in 2023–2025, compared with 2 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, permits to build new homes citywide went down 11%.
In Allentown, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $1.2M (2020–2022) to $7.2M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
Allentown had 79 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 44 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2024, when permits to build new homes rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion. Many of these permits were issued on the same day, which usually means one large multi-lot project.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
plain.similar_text: Other neighborhoods with a similar pattern: Mt. Oliver, Hazelwood, Ridgemont.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 4 scored permit indicators in Garfield moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

New residential construction permits: 30 in 2023–2025 vs. 4 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 4 would be expected. Residential renovation / alteration permits: 143 in 2023–2025 vs. 149 in 2020–2022 (-4%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 167 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: renovations (2022, lower), then new construction (2023, higher), then permit value (2023, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 348 vacant lots here (293.8 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.headline: Garfield saw far more new-home building activity than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Garfield had 30 permits to build new homes in 2023–2025, compared with 4 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, permits to build new homes citywide went down 11%.
Garfield had 143 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 149 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2023, when permits to build new homes rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 2 scored permit indicators in Esplen moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $168K in 2023–2025 vs. $40K in 2020–2022 (+321%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $44K would be expected.

Timing: permit value first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2024.

Context: the City owns 29 vacant lots here (48.1 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Esplen saw much more money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Esplen, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $40K (2020–2022) to $168K (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2024, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Low — there are few permits here or the signals are mixed, so one project can swing the numbers.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 3 of 4 scored permit indicators in Manchester moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $9.5M in 2023–2025 vs. $2.8M in 2020–2022 (+234%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $3.2M would be expected. Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 13 in 2023–2025 vs. 5 in 2020–2022 (+160%); citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 5 would be expected. Residential renovation / alteration permits: 128 in 2023–2025 vs. 75 in 2020–2022 (+71%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 84 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2022, lower), then demolitions (2023, higher), then renovations (2024, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 82 vacant lots here (113.4 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

bullets: In Manchester, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $2.8M (2020–2022) to $9.5M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
Manchester had 13 demolition permits in 2023–2025, compared with 5 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, demolition permits citywide went down 8%.
Manchester had 128 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 75 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 3 of 4 scored permit indicators in California-Kirkbride moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $656K in 2023–2025 vs. $2.0M in 2020–2022 (-67%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $2.2M would be expected. Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 0 in 2023–2025 vs. 10 in 2020–2022 (-100%); citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 9 would be expected. Residential renovation / alteration permits: 14 in 2023–2025 vs. 28 in 2020–2022 (-50%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 31 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2022, lower), then renovations (2023, lower). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 231 vacant lots here (412.3 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.headline: California-Kirkbride saw much less money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In California-Kirkbride, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $2.0M (2020–2022) to $656K (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
California-Kirkbride had 0 demolition permits in 2023–2025, compared with 10 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, demolition permits citywide went down 8%.
California-Kirkbride had 14 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 28 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2022, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) fell below what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Low — there are few permits here or the signals are mixed, so one project can swing the numbers.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 3 scored permit indicators in Duquesne Heights moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $1.4M in 2023–2025 vs. $4.4M in 2020–2022 (-67%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $4.9M would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: new construction (2023, lower), then permit value (2023, lower). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 98 vacant lots here (61.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Duquesne Heights saw much less money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Duquesne Heights, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $4.4M (2020–2022) to $1.4M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2023, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) fell below what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
plain.similar_text: Other neighborhoods with a similar pattern: Marshall-Shadeland, Chartiers City, Bon Air.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 3 scored permit indicators in Fineview moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 50 in 2023–2025 vs. 22 in 2020–2022 (+127%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 25 would be expected. Declared value of residential building permits: $1.6M in 2023–2025 vs. $722K in 2020–2022 (+126%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $802K would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2022, lower), then demolitions (2023, higher), then renovations (2023, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 251 vacant lots here (389.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Fineview saw more home renovations than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Fineview had 50 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 22 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
In Fineview, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $722K (2020–2022) to $1.6M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2023, when home renovation permits rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 3 scored permit indicators in Perry South moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 101 in 2023–2025 vs. 131 in 2020–2022 (-23%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 147 would be expected. Declared value of residential building permits: $2.9M in 2023–2025 vs. $4.7M in 2020–2022 (-38%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $5.2M would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: demolitions (2022, higher), then permit value (2022, lower), then renovations (2023, lower). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 572 vacant lots here (243.9 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.

We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 3 scored permit indicators in Central Oakland moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $758K in 2023–2025 vs. $239K in 2020–2022 (+217%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $266K would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2023, higher), then renovations (2024, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 7 vacant lots here (9.7 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Central Oakland saw much more money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Central Oakland, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $239K (2020–2022) to $758K (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2023, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 2 scored permit indicators in Ridgemont moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $216K in 2023–2025 vs. $79K in 2020–2022 (+175%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $87K would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: renovations (2022, higher), then permit value (2022, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 69 vacant lots here (72.5 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 3 of 4 scored permit indicators in South Side Slopes moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

New residential construction permits: 7 in 2023–2025 vs. 2 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 2 would be expected. Residential renovation / alteration permits: 186 in 2023–2025 vs. 129 in 2020–2022 (+44%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 145 would be expected. Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 9 in 2023–2025 vs. 5 in 2020–2022 (+80%); citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 5 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: renovations (2022, higher), then permit value (2022, higher), then new construction (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 160 vacant lots here (89.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.

Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 4 scored permit indicators in Lower Lawrenceville moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $2.8M in 2023–2025 vs. $5.1M in 2020–2022 (-44%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $5.6M would be expected. Residential renovation / alteration permits: 108 in 2023–2025 vs. 123 in 2020–2022 (-12%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 138 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: demolitions (2022, higher), then permit value (2023, lower), then renovations (2025, lower). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 28 vacant lots here (25.1 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.headline: Lower Lawrenceville saw much less money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Lower Lawrenceville, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $5.1M (2020–2022) to $2.8M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
Lower Lawrenceville had 108 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 123 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2023, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) fell below what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 3 scored permit indicators in Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $1.6M in 2023–2025 vs. $688K in 2020–2022 (+128%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $765K would be expected. Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 9 in 2023–2025 vs. 5 in 2020–2022 (+80%); citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 5 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: renovations (2024, higher), then permit value (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 319 vacant lots here (69.3 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar saw much more money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $688K (2020–2022) to $1.6M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar had 9 demolition permits in 2023–2025, compared with 5 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, demolition permits citywide went down 8%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2025, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 2 scored permit indicators in Allegheny West moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $1.9M in 2023–2025 vs. $839K in 2020–2022 (+126%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $933K would be expected.

Timing: permit value first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2022.

Context: the City owns 2 vacant lots here (5.5 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Allegheny West saw much more money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Allegheny West, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $839K (2020–2022) to $1.9M (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2022, when planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Low — there are few permits here or the signals are mixed, so one project can swing the numbers.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 2 of 4 scored permit indicators in South Side Flats moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 196 in 2023–2025 vs. 214 in 2020–2022 (-8%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 240 would be expected. Declared value of residential building permits: $4.9M in 2023–2025 vs. $6.6M in 2020–2022 (-26%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $7.4M would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: new construction (2022, higher), then demolitions (2022, higher), then permit value (2022, higher), then renovations (2024, lower). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 22 vacant lots here (9.2 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 4 scored permit indicators in Middle Hill moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Declared value of residential building permits: $710K in 2023–2025 vs. $1.2M in 2020–2022 (-43%); citywide the change was +11%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about $1.4M would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: new construction (2022, higher), then permit value (2022, higher), then demolitions (2025, lower). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 303 vacant lots here (383.4 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.headline: Middle Hill saw much less money planned for home projects than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: In Middle Hill, planned spending on home building and renovation (as declared on permits) went from $1.2M (2020–2022) to $710K (2023–2025). Over the same period, planned spending citywide went up 11%.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 2 scored permit indicators in Strip District moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 4 in 2023–2025 vs. 11 in 2020–2022 (-64%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 12 would be expected.

Timing: renovations first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2022.

Context: the City owns 3 vacant lots here (1.9 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Declared value of residential building permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Strip District saw fewer home renovations than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Strip District had 4 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 11 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2022, when home renovation permits fell below what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 4 scored permit indicators in Crawford-Roberts moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 4 in 2023–2025 vs. 1 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 1 would be expected.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: new construction (2022, higher), then permit value (2022, higher), then renovations (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 105 vacant lots here (156.6 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

plain.headline: Crawford-Roberts saw more demolitions than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Crawford-Roberts had 4 demolition permits in 2023–2025, compared with 1 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, demolition permits citywide went down 8%.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
plain.similar_text: Other neighborhoods with a similar pattern: Homewood North, Crafton Heights, Fineview.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 2 scored permit indicators in Point Breeze moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 318 in 2023–2025 vs. 319 in 2020–2022 (-0%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 358 would be expected.

Timing: renovations first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2025.

Context: the City owns 7 vacant lots here (2.7 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2025, when home renovation permits fell below what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 421 in 2023–2025 vs. 416 in 2020–2022 (+1%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 467 would be expected.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 2 scored permit indicators in Overbrook moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 116 in 2023–2025 vs. 80 in 2020–2022 (+45%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 90 would be expected.

Timing: renovations first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2023.

Context: the City owns 61 vacant lots here (28.1 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Bon Air broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2022, higher), then renovations (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 40 vacant lots here (49.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Building activity in Bon Air has broadly kept pace with the rest of Pittsburgh.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 3 scored permit indicators in Brookline moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 463 in 2023–2025 vs. 357 in 2020–2022 (+30%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 401 would be expected.

Timing: renovations first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2025.

Context: the City owns 182 vacant lots here (33.7 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Brookline saw more home renovations than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Brookline had 463 home renovation permits in 2023–2025, compared with 357 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, home renovation permits citywide went up 12%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2025, when home renovation permits rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
plain.similar_text: Other neighborhoods with a similar pattern: Overbrook, Swisshelm Park, Westwood.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Carrick broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: demolitions (2022, lower), then renovations (2025, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 149 vacant lots here (34.4 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Building activity in Carrick has broadly kept pace with the rest of Pittsburgh.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
plain.similar_text: Other neighborhoods with a similar pattern: Westwood, Windgap, Greenfield.
plain.market: In ZIP 15210, which covers about 81% of this neighborhood: Home values rose 8% (2020–2022 to 2023–2025; typical county ZIP: +14%); Asking rents rose 21% (Aug 2023 to Aug 2026; typical county ZIP: +14%).

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 3 scored permit indicators in Spring Hill-City View moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Residential renovation / alteration permits: 56 in 2023–2025 vs. 65 in 2020–2022 (-14%); citywide the change was +12%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 73 would be expected.

Context: the City owns 203 vacant lots here (124.1 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Central Lawrenceville broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Context: the City owns 3 vacant lots here (1.2 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Morningside broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Timing: permit value first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2023.

Context: the City owns 20 vacant lots here (20.3 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Marshall-Shadeland broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Timing: demolitions first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2022.

Context: the City owns 151 vacant lots here (46.6 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.

Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Brighton Heights broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Context: the City owns 153 vacant lots here (52.5 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Building activity in Brighton Heights has broadly kept pace with the rest of Pittsburgh.
plain.confidence: Medium — this is based on one source (City building permits), so treat it as a lead rather than a conclusion.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Larimer broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Context: the City owns 446 vacant lots here (386.9 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in Stanton Heights broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Context: the City owns 40 vacant lots here (20.9 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
