finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 1 scored permit indicators in Central Business District moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 5 in 2023–2025 vs. 1 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 1 would be expected.

Timing: demolitions first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2024.

Context: the City owns 10 vacant lots here (6.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.
New residential construction permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Residential renovation / alteration permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.
Declared value of residential building permits: UNKNOWN — too few permits to score.

plain.headline: Central Business District saw more demolitions than the city trend would suggest.
bullets: Central Business District had 5 demolition permits in 2023–2025, compared with 1 in 2020–2022. Over the same period, demolition permits citywide went down 8%.
plain.timing: This pattern first showed up in 2024, when demolition permits rose above what this neighborhood's earlier share of city activity would suggest. Timing alone doesn't tell us why things changed.
plain.confidence: Low — there are few permits here or the signals are mixed, so one project can swing the numbers. Many of these permits were issued on the same day, which usually means one large multi-lot project.
keep_in_mind: Permits show plans to build, renovate or demolish — not finished homes.
We don't yet have neighborhood data on rents, home prices, incomes or who lives here.
Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, 1 of 1 scored permit indicators in South Shore moved noticeably differently from the citywide pattern.

Demolition permits (complete + city-funded): 4 in 2023–2025 vs. 1 in 2020–2022; citywide the change was -8%. Had it followed the citywide trend, about 1 would be expected.

Context: the City owns 19 vacant lots here (36.0 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

Taken together, the permit record indicates that building activity in this neighborhood changed differently from the rest of the city during this period.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in North Shore broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Timing: demolitions first departed from its 2020–21 share of city activity in 2025.

Context: the City owns 13 vacant lots here (16.4 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

finding.text:
Between 2020–2022 and 2023–2025, permit activity in West End broadly followed the citywide pattern; no scored indicator stood out strongly.

Timing: the first departures from 2020–21 patterns appeared in this order: permit value (2022, higher), then renovations (2022, higher). This ordering is evidence about timing only; it does not show that one change produced another.

Context: the City owns 47 vacant lots here (90.7 per km² vs. 63.0 citywide), from a 2026-09-24 snapshot.

The available evidence does not establish why these changes happened, whether permitted work was completed, or how rents, prices or residents were affected: no neighborhood-level rent, sales, income or vacancy-rate data is loaded.

limitations: No dataset in this analysis establishes causal relationships.
A permit being issued does not mean construction started or was completed; permits do not record how many homes are created.
No neighborhood-level rent, home price, income, household or vacancy-rate data is loaded, so Sherlock cannot say how residents or housing costs were affected.
City-owned vacant lots come from a single snapshot and exclude privately owned vacant land.
The City changed permit systems in 2024. Work types were mapped to common categories, but counting practices may differ before and after.
Neighborhood boundaries are built from 2010 Census blocks; the permit file's own neighborhood labels are used to assign permits.
Metro context comes from Zillow's 7-county Pittsburgh metro area and does not describe this neighborhood.
2019 (from June) and 2026 (through 2026-09-21) are partial years and are excluded from change calculations.

Unusual doesn't mean good or bad — it means different from the rest of the city.
